items.name: Elasticsearch and Lucene
items.explanation: Elasticsearch is a search engine that spreads an index over many nodes. It is built on Lucene, the library that builds and reads the indexes on each node.

assumedBy.quote: When we first deployed Elasticsearch, it took months to index all of the code on GitHub (about 8 million repositories at the time).
Each of our Elasticsearch indices is a single Lucene index under the hood

items.name: Regular expressions
items.explanation: A pattern that matches runs of characters, such as arguments? for argument or arguments. A search system cannot look up a pattern directly, so it has to turn it into pieces an index can answer.

assumedBy.quote: Here, you can see that the regex gets translated into a series of substring queries on the ngram indices.

items.name: Kafka topics, partitions and offsets
items.explanation: Kafka keeps messages in an ordered log per topic, split into partitions. A reader tracks its place with an offset, so it can resume or replay from any point.

assumedBy.quote: Kafka provides events that tell us to go index something.

items.name: Kubernetes operators
items.explanation: An operator is a program that runs inside Kubernetes and manages another application for you, handling setup, upgrades and replacement of failed pieces.

assumedBy.quote: Now that we had committed to running on Kubernetes and using the ECK operator, we envisioned a more expansive architecture where we ran a larger number of smaller Elasticsearch clusters.

items.name: Publish and subscribe
items.explanation: Senders publish a message to a topic and everyone subscribed to it receives a copy, without the sender knowing who they are.

assumedBy.quote: In fact, the convenience of PubSub’s guaranteed message delivery led us to adopt PubSub for other use cases across Discord like task scheduling
